paper_title: BEND 2.0: Benchmarking the Capabilities Needed to Design DNA

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Genomic foundation models are increasingly used to propose DNA sequences and edits. But successful design requires capabilities that current benchmarks do not measure. Here we introduce BEND 2.0 (BENchmark for DNA language models), which tests how well models predict the effects of DNA changes and whether these predictions can guide sequence design. Across eight tasks built on five experimental datasets, we find that model choice and how representations are accessed both affect performance. Linear readouts fitted to frozen representations can match or exceed models' native outputs, and functional post-training substantially improves the models' capabilities. Linear readouts transfer well across experimental assays and genes, suggesting that models capture functional patterns beyond the data used to fit individual predictors. At the same time, strong prediction of average effects can conceal weaker prediction of context-specific effects, and accurate prediction of combined mutation effects does not imply accurate prediction of their interactions. In design tasks, model predictions can reduce the number of candidates needed to find a desired response, but still leave substantial room for better design choices, particularly for context-specific and multi-cell objectives. Our benchmark reveals that genomic models now display signs of general utility but have yet to saturate on performance in even simple tasks.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: A biologist seeking to change the activity of regulatory sequence may have hundreds of mutations to choose from. The same mutation can have different effects in different cell types or even on slightly different genetic background. To help choose what to test, models must distinguish small changes most likely to produce fine-grained desired response. Genomic models use different approaches to learn the complex and multifaceted patterns encoded in DNA, drawing on both sequence diversity and measurements of biological function. Models such as Evo2 and DNABERT-2 learn from natural sequence variation (Brixi et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2024), while GPN-Star uses evolutionary relationships to predict functional constraint (Ye et al., 2026). Other models incorporate functional outcomes rather than relying on natural sequence variation and homology. AlphaGenome, for example, predicts expression, accessibility and splicing from functional genomic data (Avsec et al., 2026), while NTv3 combines sequence learning with such functional supervision (Boshar et al., 2025). Foundation models and task-specific models have guided the design of sequences with cell type-targeted activity (Gosai et al., 2024) and, more recently, viable bacteriophage genomes (King et al., 2026). However, the central question remains: which features of sequence and function have these models learned well enough to guide experiments?

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Looking only at overall predictive accuracy leaves that question unanswered. sequence-based score may identify mutation at an evolutionarily constrained position without predicting its effect on expression in particular cell type. Accurate predictions for individual mutations do not establish whether model captures interactions between mutations or can predict their effects on different genetic background. Similarly, distinguishing highly active genes from weakly active genes does not indicate which edit will produce desired change in expression. Each of these cases calls for more precise testing. Building on BEND (Marin et al., 2024), we introduce BEND 2.0 to test whether genomic models can guide DNA design. The benchmark is organized around five key capabilities: Prior, Function, Context, Interaction, and Design. Together, our tasks measure what genomic models can predict and whether they can help select DNA sequences that produce desired response. Table 1 summarizes our selected evaluations. Related works. The original BEND benchmark (Marin et al., 2024), GenBench (Liu et al., 2024), and OmniGenBench (Yang et al., 2025) provide systematic evaluations of genomic representations across downstream tasks. In parallel, model-guided regulatory sequence design has demonstrated cell type-targeted activity experimentally (Gosai et al., 2024; Yin et al., 2025; Castillo-Hair et al., 2025), and NucleoBench (Shor et al., 2025) evaluates algorithms for searching sequence space using predictive models as scoring functions. BEND 2.0 connects these directions by testing the predictive distinctions that highly matter for design: resolving context-specific effects, predicting interactions between mutations, and distinguishing candidates with different functional outcomes. sections.title: 3 SEQUENCE PRIORS: MEASURING WHAT MODELS KNOW ABOUT DNA
sections.content: The models learn useful sequence priors. To compare causal and masked sequence models, we mask out the central base of 512 GRCh38 windows of 1,200bp. For this base reconstruction, NTv3 650M post and Evo2 have the lowest losses among models in Figure 1A. The foundation models outperform simple base composition statistics, but do not seem to have converged on prediction accuracy. For all NTv3 models, we used fixed 12% additional masking from its training objective, and the final scores averaged the central-base loss over two draws.

sections.title: 4 FUNCTIONAL PREDICTION: FROM SEQUENCE TO EXPERIMENTAL RESPONSE
sections.content: Mutation-effect prediction transfers. Next, we explore whether genomic models can predict how mutations affect RNA splicing. OpenSplice measures changes in exon inclusion across 590,104 mutations in 466 genes (Quarantani et al., 2026). On held-out genes, AlphaGenomes embeddingfitted linear head reaches macro-gene Spearman 0.650, compared with 0.621 for its native outputs and 0.564 for NTv3 650M post (Figure 2A). An older specialist model SpliceAI (Jaganathan et al., 2019) reaches 0.674, higher than the top-performing foundation models. NTv3 enables comparison of the same architecture before and after functional training (posttraining). Post-training improves mutation-effect prediction at both model sizes, and the readout from the 650M post-trained model significantly outperforms both readout from the matched architecture 4 BEND 2.

sections.title: 5 BIOLOGICAL CONTEXT: HOW DOES FUNCTION DEPEND ON THE CONTEXT
sections.content: Mutation effects differ between cells. Models may easily predict mutations average effect yet struggle to predict such effect when conditioned on the biological context. Commonly, one may be interested in specific tissues or cell types. In the Siraj dataset, the same mutations are measured in both HepG2 and K562 cells, allowing us to evaluate both their mean effect and the difference between cell types (Siraj et al., 2026). Across 128 regulatory elements, AlphaGenome predicts the mean effect with correlation of 0.532, compared with 0.398 for the difference between them (Figure 3A/B). It uses its existing prediction tracks without fitting to Siraj measurements. Linear readouts fitted to NTv3 650M post reach 0.492 and 0.256, respectively. Both models predict the mean more accurately than the difference, with larger gap for NTv3.

sections.title: 6 GENETIC INTERACTIONS: PREDICTING DEPARTURES FROM ADDITIVITY
sections.content: A mutations effect depends on its genetic background. Rather than the cell level context of the previous section, different genetic backgrounds may also alter the effect of mutations. The Siraj data allows for isolating this interaction, since it contains the same edit on two paired allelic backgrounds. Across 68,026 paired mutations in 114 regulatory elements, AlphaGenome reaches interaction correlation 0.260, compared with 0.187 for NTv3 650M posts fitted readout and 0.181 for Enformer (Avsec et al., 2021) (Figure 4A). Predictions are most accurate for mutations within 10 bp of one another and become less accurate with increasing separation (Figure 4C). Combined-effect accuracy can conceal weak interaction prediction. COMPASS tests nonadditive interactions on splicing by measuring single and double mutations relative to the same reference. On its 110-gene panel, NTv3 650M post reaches correlation 0.409 for single-mutation effects and 0.500 for double-mutation effects, but only 0.046 for the interaction remaining after subtracting the two single effects (Figure 4B). Native splice predictors show the same pattern, and replicate correlation for the interaction measurements is 0.171. To assess how much interaction prediction contributes to overall accuracy, we remove the predicted interaction and retain only the additive effects. NTv3s double-mutation correlation changes only from 0.500 to 0.493. Similarly, removing AlphaGenomes predicted background dependence on Siraj changes overall correlation from 0.528 to 0.521, small but statistically supported decrease of 0.0070 (95% interval: 0.00140.0120; Appendix E.2). This indicates that model can predict combined effects accurately while recovering little of the interaction between mutations. 6 BEND 2.

sections.title: 7 GENOMIC DESIGN: SELECTING SEQUENCES FOR A DESIRED RESPONSE
sections.content: We finally ask whether model predictions help choose DNA with desired response. These tasks evaluate the measured outcomes of model-selected candidates, progressing from matching single response to controlling expression across multiple cell types. All choices are made within experimentally assayed libraries, with candidate measurements withheld from selection. Matching target response. Can model find an alternative mutation that reproduces the effect of reference edit? In the Siraj assay, each element contains natural variant and measured change in activity, which we define as the target response. Excluding that position leaves 578597 candidate substitutions per element. model predicts an effect for every candidate and the reference edit, then ranks candidates by how closely their predicted effects match its own reference prediction. AlphaGenome scores effects as changes in its cell-matched accessibility outputs; NTv3 uses linear heads evaluated on held-out elements. All candidates measured effects are withheld until scoring. For evaluation, we rank edits by how closely their measured effects match the target. Across 331 targets in 110 elements, AlphaGenomes first choice has an average percentile rank of 24.3, compared with 30.0 for NTv3 650M post and 50 for uniform selection (Figure 5A; lower is better). The top ten choices include at least one edit that matches the reference response within assay uncertainty for 62% of targets with AlphaGenome and 59% with NTv3, compared with 38% under uniform selection (Figure 5B). Model rankings can therefore help find matching edits with fewer tests. Changing expression selectively. We also test more challenging task, choosing edits which increase expression in one cell type while minimally changing expression in another. We evaluate 167,958 substitutions across 280 parental backgrounds at 127 Siraj loci, with HepG2 and K562 alternately serving as the target cell. Each model chooses one substitution or no edit by maximizing predicted utility Ucell = λo, where and are expression changes relative to the unmutated parent in the target and other cell. Six fixed penalties describe the tradeoff between the two responses (Figure 5C). Complete loci were held out of readout fitting and native-output calibration.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSIONS
sections.content: Genomic models capture functional information that transfers across datasets and genes. This genomic understanding helps them select DNA with desired target response. Functional training largely expands these capabilities: predictions from embedding-fitted linear heads also match or exceed native outputs, suggesting that its benefits extend beyond the prediction heads and affect the models more deeply. At the same time, accurate aggregate predictions can conceal weak understanding of cell types and genetic interactions, which on the other hand are highly important for practical downstream use. BEND 2.0 focuses on the capabilities that matter for genomic design, hoping to support the development of models that make this search more effective.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Tasks with less consistent experimental results are often the more difficult tasks for the models, meaning performance should be interpreted in light of the experiments reliability. The chosen experimental references are somewhat naive (for example, transferring mutation effects across cell types), yet they still beat current models. The linear heads may also depend on the embedding sizes of the models, and models with different input context lengths may have an effect on task performance. Despite these limits, BEND 2.0 shows where genomic models may help narrow hundreds of candidate mutations to testable few, and where further progress is needed.

ETHICS STATEMENT This work evaluates machine learning models using existing functional-genomics experiments, reference sequences and population-genomic resources. Human genomic data can be identifying. We used the data in accordance with the applicable access and redistribution conditions, which also govern future use. Performance on the contexts presented here should not be assumed to generalize uniformly to other populations or biological settings. Models supporting genomic design may also have dual-use applications. Downstream use therefore requires appropriate biological validation, biosafety review and oversight. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT We provide all code and fixed data splits for running BEND 2.0. We also host the benchmarking data in our own Hugging Face repository so future evaluations do not depend on the original hosts, making our benchmark more sturdy. Data are redistributed under their original terms, with attribution and licensing information included in the repository. Our code includes both setup and evaluation instructions, while our appendices contain additional methodological details and supporting results.

For experimental references, we use one set of measurements to make predictions or choose sequences, then evaluate these predictions or choices using another set. Depending on the setting, the references can be somewhat naive (for example, transferring effects across cell types) or stronger (predicting the same response using repeat measurements). The split is dependent on the experimental data: For OpenSplice, we compare the average of two variant PSI repeats with the third, averaging all three rotations. Effects share the reported wild-type estimate. For Siraj, the background-interaction reference compares measurements between HepG2 and K562. Other references compare effects calculated separately from repeats 12 and 35. We evaluate model predictions against effects estimated from all repeats. For cell-selective design, we instead evaluate both model choices and experimental references using effects relative to the unmutated parent. For GTEx, tissue identification averages both donor-half directions (99.0%), and its uncertainty was not re-estimated. For Atlas, each of the two RNA measurements is evaluated against the other. For the Siraj data, the references for cell effects use 127 of the 128 Siraj elements, as one lacks the required count data. Ranking and target-response matching use all 331 targets in 110 elements. We select on one repeat group, test on the other, then swap the groups and average the results. Uncertainty and scoring. B.1 HOW POST-TRAINING CHANGES ACCESS TO THE SEQUENCE PRIOR Additional masking improves base prediction in post-trained NTv3 despite somewhat counterintuitively removing more of the surrounding DNA context (Figure 1B). We investigate this effect and test whether the improved performance can be reproduced while only masking the target base. Mask placement. We test both NTv3 sizes before and after post-training on the 512 benchmark windows. Each query masks the target base and alters 144 other positions, using two random draws. Masks are spread across the window, placed within 128 bases of the target, or kept more than 256 bases away. For distant masks, we compare scattered and compact patterns with the same number of masks on each side and matched average distances. We also replace the same distant bases with other nucleotides instead of MASK tokens. For 650M post, distant scattered masks give lower loss than compact masks (1.794 versus 2.167 bits; paired difference 0.373, 95% interval 0.2830.467). Mask count and average distance therefore do not explain the difference. Base replacement does not reproduce the benefit. The 100M post model behaves similarly, while pre-trained models change much less (Figure 8AB). Replacing transformer representations. NTv3 predicts bases using both its final transformer representation and convolutional features that bypass the transformer (skip features) (Boshar et al., 2025). With only the target base masked, we replace the transformer representation with one obtained from the same DNA with extra masks or base replacements. We keep the skip features fixed, then test the reverse: replacing only the skip features. For 650M post, uniform masking lowers loss by 0.821 bits. Replacing only the transformer representation reproduces 0.812 bits of this improvement. Replacing only the skip features changes loss by +0.014 bits, with an interval that includes zero. We exclude any overlapping sequences and remove the 23 shared genes from both datasets. The CNN and ResNet use 398 OpenSplice genes for training and another 45 for validation. Trivially, COMPASS measurements are not used for any kind of model selection, but only for evaluation. Learning from fewer examples. We vary the number of measured OpenSplice variants used to fit the NTv3 linear readouts and train the one-hot CNN. The models use the same training subsets and are evaluated on the same held-out genes. NTv3 readouts greatly outperform the CNN at every tested training-set size, showing strong gains from the use of foundation models (Figure 10). t r a t F Figure 10: OpenSplice prediction with fewer assay labels. Larger training subsets include the smaller ones. Lines show the mean across three runs with different training samples and seeds while the shading shows their range. The training-set sizes count only OpenSplice examples. NTv3 post was previously trained on functional genomic data. Direction and magnitude of mutation effects. For mutations that have clearly measured effects (PSI > 1.96σ, where σ is the reported measurement uncertainty), the NTv3 650M post readout correctly predicts whether exon inclusion increases or decreases in 74.1% of cases, compared with 69.2% for the one-hot ResNet. Across all mutations, their root mean square errors (adjusted for measurement noise) are respectively 16.55 and 17.27 percentage points. We calculate each metric within genes and then average across genes. NTv3s mean calibration slope is 0.98 (95% interval: 0.951.01), close to the ideal value of one, indicating that predicted effects are on very similar scale to the measured effects. C.1 CHANGING FOCUS FROM PREDICTING EFFECTS TO ATTEMPTING AN EDIT Predicting mutation and edit effects is only part of DNA design: we also need to perform the edit efficiently. We next test whether genomic models can predict how editing efficiency varies with the surrounding DNA. Experimental setting. We use the K562 TRIP dataset from PRIDICT2 (Mathis et al., 2025), which places 640-bp reporter at 1,196 locations across 23 chromosomes. Editing efficiency is measured for prime editing, adenine editing (ABE8e-SpG), cytosine editing (BE4max) and Cas9 (SpCas9). Prime editing uses one fixed guide while the other three systems share another. Prediction and evaluation. Models receive the same 8-kb reference-genome window around each integration site (without the inserted reporter). We fit separate ridge readout to each models frozen embeddings for each editing system. Training and testing use five cross-validation splits, keeping complete chromosomes together. Features are scaled using the training data, and the ridge penalty is fixed at α = 1000. We additionally check whether the results depend on this penalty by choosing α {1, 10, . . . , 109} through three-fold cross-validation within the training chromosomes.
